extracted.intended_audience: architects, masons, builders, and students of architecture (and informed general readers interested in masonry design)
extracted.subtask_short: design wall cornices and pier bases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and proportioning wall cornices (including dripstones and bracket/roof cornices) and the bases of piers/columns, with rules on form, material, and aesthetic expression tied to function and climate. Emphasises primitive types (X and Y), structural adaptations, and visual expression of security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice two offices (roof or hand)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cornice has one of two offices: if the wall has nothing to carry, the cornice is its roof and defends it from the weather; if there is weight to be carried above the wall, the cornice is its hand and is expanded to carry the said weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose cornice form according to intended function: protective (weatherproofing) or load-distributing (support). All subsequent design choices must respect which office the cornice serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect unfinished wall tops with projecting flat stones
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect the top of an unfinished wall from rain and to distribute point loads, lay a great flat stone (or a series) projecting well over the edge of the wall veil to receive and spread any weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple protective/distributional cap is the practical starting point for the cornice; failure to provide such projection leaves joints exposed to weather and frost damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of two constant cornice members: sloped (X) and upright (Y)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bevelled or sloping stone is denoted X, and the upright edged stone Y; these two members are ‘constant’ and fundamental in cornice construction and analogous to similar members in bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the relation and roles of X and Y in mind: X is the sloping element (intersection of slopes), Y the upright element (perpendicular with two slopes). Many forms are developed from their relations; designers should refer to these primitives repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root/primal cornice form as basis for variation
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a primal cornice type (root form) from which families of cornices are developed by modifying the profile of X (hollowing inward or bulging outward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the root form as inviolable primitive; allowable invention lies in curvature, slope, and proportion — not in altering the primitive relation of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two main cornice families: hollow (dripstone) and bulging (true cornice)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the root form spring two vast families: one (hollowed X) to keep rain off (dripstone), the other (bulged X) to strengthen for carrying weight (true cornice); a third combined group arises from aesthetic combinations of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select family based on climate and structural needs; vary slope of the root line, depths of X and Y, and curve nature according to weight, stone strength, cornice size, and aesthetic law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt slope/curve/proportion to weight, material, size, and aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: The slope of the root line and nature of the curves (here drawn as circle segments) vary according to the weight to be carried, strength of the stone, size of the cornice, and aesthetic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers have latitude in these parameters, but must remain within functional limits: heavier loads demand sturdier proportions; delicate aesthetics must not compromise protective or supportive function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose true cornice vs dripstone by climate and ornament visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If climate is fine and rain not frequent, prefer the true cornice (which favors decoration); if rain is frequent and freezing alternates, adopt a protective dripstone that hollows X farther to prevent rain damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that hollowing X too much will hide ornament in shadow; the dripstone sacrifices the cornice's crown/ornament character for protection and is characteristic of Northern (Gothic) architecture, while the true cornice suits Southern (Greek/Italian) architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight advancement of the upper ledge to assist protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither hollowed nor bulging forms are perfectly protective, but slight advance/cutting off of the sharp upper point and slight advancement of the upper stone can improve protection (forms f and g, characteristic of early Byzantine work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor modifications (cutting off weak points, advancing upper stones) can materially improve weather resistance while maintaining decorative visibility; use historically-proven variants (Byzantine examples) as references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dripstone essential detail: up-and-under cutting and roll projection
rubrics_metrics.description: For effective dripstone, boldly hollow X upwards (up-cut) and cut the whole from a single stone; round off and let the stone project in a roll so water does not lodge on the upper ledge; often shaped into a falcon’s beak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential arrangement is the up-and-under cutting of the curve; the dripstone moulding is a clear indicator of builders accustomed to wet climates. Use single-stone carving where possible to achieve the undercut without weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undercut mouldings indicate wet-climate influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever we find up-cut or under-cut curve in mouldings, it indicates a wet climate or that builders have been bred in a wet country; such undercutting can distinguish regional influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence of undercut as a diagnostic for stylistic/historical attribution (e.g., Lombardic influence, Northern vs Arab/Byzantine types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket (roof) cornices for carrying substantial weight or galleries
rubrics_metrics.description: If the weight above becomes considerable or cornice must project far and carry weight (e.g., a gallery on top), support the cornice at intervals with brackets; this family (bracket-cornice) is essentially connected with roofs and galleries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place brackets on a plain cornice without superincumbent weight (unless for stylistic reasons); the presence of brackets should imply a roof or gallery above. Treat roof cornices separately from wall cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piers as 'gathered up' walls to sustain vertical pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a wall must sustain large vertical pressure, the wall is 'gathered up' into piers—coagulated wall—concentrating material into discrete supports (piers/columns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the analogy (paper rolled into tubes) to justify concentrating wall material into piers to increase load-bearing capacity without increasing material quantity unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan form for piers: circle (pillar/column) concentrates strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing every particle of the pier as near as possible to its centre yields the circle; the circle is therefore the best possible plan form for a pier—hence pillars/columns are ideal for vertical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer circular (columnar) plans when vertical load-bearing efficiency is desired; transformations from square to circular allow material savings while increasing effective strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate wall base/cornice into column base/capital when concentrated
rubrics_metrics.description: The wall base is cut to pieces and gathered and becomes the base of the column; the wall cornice becomes the capital of the column. Thus base, veil (shaft), and cornice concentrate into base, shaft, and capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting wall elements into column elements, preserve relative profiles and proportions appropriately scaled; understand capitals as concentrated cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill intervals between piers in foundation to prevent differential settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: When foundations are cut to pieces into piers, pressure is thrown on narrowed detached areas; fill intervals between piers so the whole foundation bonds into one and will sink together if it sinks at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important where ground has variable bearing; Greek best practice fills intervals up to the root of the shaft so columns stand on an even foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express security to the eye as part of good architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Features necessary to express security to the imagination are often as essential as those required for security itself; a slender column may need an independent base or socket to look balanced and held to the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must attend to the visual expression of stability (expanded or divided bases, claws/spurs) even where real structural necessity is small, because perception influences architectural success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pier base composition: square block Yb with circular Xb and corner spurs
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and pleasing pier base combines a square block (Yb) enclosing the circular member (Xb), with triangular spurs/props sloping from the square's corners to Xb to give an appearance of grasp and firm hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The triangular spur form expresses support most effectively to the eye; although these spurs are almost useless structurally, they materially increase the perceived security. Forms combining square and circle are both practical and aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material rule: use single stone blocks for concentrated base members
rubrics_metrics.description: As the whole weight of the building is to rest upon a few limited spaces, Xb and Yb are, if possible, to be each of a single stone; when the shaft is small, both may be cut from one block to give a surface free from joints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-block members avoid joints beneath shaft and present a firm covering over smaller masonry; prefer solid masonry where loads concentrate to reduce risk and improve visual unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion limit for Yb (base height relative to width)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Yb looks so thin that the column above might break it, it is too low; if Yb is higher than its own width, it is too high. The utmost admissible height is that of a cubic block.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain base height within limits: avoid overly low or overly tall bases; as a general rule, height of Yb should not exceed its width (max = cubic block) to avoid the base becoming part of the pier rather than its foot.
